DKA; start isotonic IV fluids and an IV insulin infusion per protocol after checking potassium, and monitor for cerebral edema
rationale: Hyperglycemia with ketosis and metabolic acidosis plus fruity breath and Kussmaul respirations defines DKA, which can occur at glucose levels below 500 and even near normal in euglycemic DKA. Treatment is isotonic fluids, insulin after potassium assessment, electrolyte replacement, and a search for precipitants.
stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and Kussmaul respirations. Glucose is 480 mg/dL, pH 7.24, HCO3 12 mEq/L, and ketones are large. What is the diagnosis and priority?

options: Start insulin immediately; the potassium is fine
Hold insulin and replace potassium first, per protocol often until K exceeds 3.3, because insulin will drop potassium further and risk lethal dysrhythmia
Give bicarbonate instead
Discharge the patient
rationale: Insulin and acidosis correction drive potassium intracellularly, so starting insulin with K below 3.3 risks severe hypokalemia and cardiac arrest. Potassium is replaced first per DKA protocol, and insulin begins once potassium is safe.
stem: A DKA patient has K 3.2 mEq/L before the insulin infusion starts. What is the action?

options: Stop insulin because glucose is normal
Continue insulin without dextrose until glucose is below 100
Switch to subcutaneous insulin immediately
Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue insulin until the ketoacidosis resolves; this prevents hypoglycemia while clearing ketones
rationale: When glucose falls to about 200 to 250 during DKA treatment, dextrose is added and insulin continued until the anion gap closes and acidosis resolves. Stopping insulin early allows relapse, and transition to subcutaneous insulin happens only after resolution with an overlap period.
stem: A DKA patient on an insulin infusion now has glucose 210 mg/dL with a closing anion gap and clinical improvement. What is next?

options: HHS has severe ketoacidosis
DKA always has higher osmolality
HHS involves profound hyperglycemia over 600, hyperosmolality, minimal ketosis and acidosis, and severe dehydration with altered mentation; DKA involves ketosis with significant metabolic acidosis
They are identical
rationale: HHS is defined by extreme hyperglycemia, serum osmolality above 320, and minimal ketones, occurring most often in older adults with type 2 diabetes, while DKA is defined by ketoacidosis. The distinction drives different fluid and insulin strategies and complication vigilance.
stem: What is the key distinguishing feature of HHS versus DKA?

options: This is normal DKA recovery
Cerebral edema, a rare but often fatal DKA complication; slow or stop fluids, elevate the head, notify the provider urgently, and prepare for mannitol or hypertonic saline per protocol
Give more fluids rapidly
This is only hypoglycemia
rationale: Neurologic deterioration during DKA treatment with headache, bradycardia, and altered consciousness suggests cerebral edema until proven otherwise. Fluids are slowed, the head elevated, and hyperosmolar therapy prepared. More fluids worsen edema.
stem: A 19-year-old with DKA on treatment develops headache, bradycardia, and altered level of consciousness. What is the concern?

options: Infection, along with missed insulin, new-onset diabetes, myocardial infarction, and pancreatitis; obtain cultures and an ECG and review insulin adherence
No workup is needed
Only dehydration causes DKA
Antibiotics are never indicated in DKA
rationale: Infection is the most common DKA precipitant, so every DKA admission needs a cause hunt including infection, ischemia, nonadherence, and pancreatitis. Treating only the glucose without finding the trigger invites recurrence.
stem: A DKA patient should always be evaluated for a precipitant. What is most common?

options: This is not DKA because glucose is too low
Euglycemic DKA; SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose, so hold the drug and treat as DKA
Hypoglycemia
Normal lab variation
rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to euglycemic DKA with glucose often below 250, while other diagnostic criteria remain identical. Missing the diagnosis because glucose looks acceptable is the classic error, and the drug must be held.
stem: A patient on empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, has glucose 210 mg/dL, nausea, pH 7.28, and positive ketones. What is the diagnosis?

options: DKA
Hypoglycemia
Normal aging changes
HHS, with severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality above 320, minimal ketosis, and altered mentation in older type 2 diabetes
rationale: Glucose near 1000 with hyperosmolality of 340, minimal ketones, near-normal pH, and altered mentation meets HHS criteria. Profound dehydration drives the hyperosmolality and neuro changes, distinguishing it from DKA.
stem: A 78-year-old with type 2 diabetes has 3 days of polyuria and is now lethargic. Glucose is 980 mg/dL, Na 150 mEq/L, osmolality 340, pH 7.36, and ketones are trace. What is the diagnosis?

options: Aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation first to correct profound dehydration and hyperosmolality; insulin follows volume restoration unless severe hyperkalemia or acidosis is present
Insulin bolus immediately before fluids
Fluid restriction
Hypertonic saline
rationale: HHS patients are profoundly volume depleted, and fluids alone substantially lower glucose through rehydration and improved perfusion. Giving insulin before volume restoration risks cardiovascular collapse and overly rapid osmolar shifts.
stem: What is the treatment priority in HHS?

options: Lower osmolality as fast as possible
Target a glucose drop of 200 mg/dL per hour
Correct gradually, with glucose falling about 50 to 75 mg/dL per hour and osmolality declining no more than 3 mOsm/kg per hour; too-rapid correction risks cerebral edema
No monitoring is needed
rationale: Rapid osmolar shifts in HHS cause cerebral edema, so correction is deliberately gradual with frequent neurologic checks and electrolyte monitoring. Aggressive correction does not improve outcomes and increases harm.
stem: What is safe correction in HHS?

options: The HHS patient with new chest pain and dyspnea, suggesting possible MI or PE because HHS is prothrombotic
The stable DKA patient on protocol
The hypoglycemia patient now resolved with glucose 110
The diabetic patient awaiting discharge teaching
rationale: HHS creates a markedly prothrombotic state with high risk of MI, stroke, pulmonary embolism, and mesenteric ischemia, so new cardiopulmonary symptoms need emergent evaluation. The other patients are stable.
stem: Which patient should the nurse prioritize above the others?

options: Never; fluids only
After initial fluid resuscitation restores perfusion, often after 1 to 2 liters, then a low-dose insulin infusion if glucose is not falling adequately with fluids alone
Large IV bolus immediately on arrival
Only after full resolution
rationale: Volume is restored first because fluids alone drop glucose significantly in HHS. Insulin is added once the patient is perfused if glucose remains high, avoiding the hypotension and overly rapid osmolar fall of premature insulin.
stem: When is insulin started in HHS?

options: HHS has no mortality risk
Only young patients die from HHS
HHS mortality of roughly 10 to 20 percent exceeds that of DKA, driven by age, comorbidities, and the precipitating illness; prevention through sick-day rules and hydration is key teaching
Insulin prevents all complications
rationale: HHS kills more often than DKA because it strikes older, comorbid patients and is frequently diagnosed late. Sick-day management including holding SGLT2 inhibitors and diuretics when ill, staying hydrated, and monitoring glucose prevents recurrence.
stem: An older adult asks about the dangers of HHS. What is accurate teaching?

options: Give insulin
Start a D5W infusion
Give glucagon IM
Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or juice, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat per the 15-15 rule
rationale: A conscious patient who can swallow is treated with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate with rechecking in 15 minutes per the 15-15 rule. Glucagon and IV dextrose are reserved for patients who are unconscious or cannot swallow safely, and insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.
stem: A 68-year-old diabetic patient is shaky and sweaty with glucose 58 mg/dL, conscious and able to swallow. What is the action?

options: Pour juice into the mouth
Give subcutaneous insulin
Do not give anything orally; give glucagon IM or nasally, or IV dextrose per protocol, position safely, and notify the provider
Wait for the patient to wake up
rationale: An unconscious patient cannot protect the airway, so oral intake risks aspiration. Glucagon or IV dextrose raises glucose safely, followed by investigating the cause such as missed meals, excess insulin, or renal failure prolonging insulin clearance.
stem: A patient is found unconscious with glucose 32 mg/dL and takes insulin. What is the action?

options: This is hypoglycemia unawareness; strict avoidance of lows for several weeks can restore awareness, so check glucose before driving and more frequently
Warning signs will always return immediately
Drive without checking glucose
No action is needed
rationale: Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulatory responses, erasing warning symptoms, but meticulous avoidance of lows for weeks can restore awareness. Driving and safety counseling are essential because unrecognized lows cause accidents.
stem: A patient with recurrent hypoglycemia no longer feels warning symptoms. What is the teaching?

options: One treatment is always enough
Sulfonylureas cause only brief hypoglycemia
Discharge immediately
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia can recur for 24 hours or more, so observe the patient, consider octreotide per orders, and review the medication, especially with renal impairment or missed meals
rationale: Long-acting sulfonylureas cause prolonged and recurrent hypoglycemia requiring extended monitoring, and octreotide suppresses insulin secretion in refractory cases. Renal impairment prolongs drug clearance, increasing risk in older adults.
stem: A 72-year-old on glipizide had glucose 45 mg/dL, was treated, and recovered. What is the concern?

options: Dawn phenomenon only
Nocturnal hypoglycemia with a possible Somogyi effect, meaning rebound morning hyperglycemia after an overnight low; check a 2 to 3 AM glucose to differentiate from dawn phenomenon
Normal diabetes course
Increase the evening insulin
rationale: Night sweats and morning headaches suggest overnight lows, and a 3 AM glucose distinguishes Somogyi effect, low at 3 AM with rebound morning high, from dawn phenomenon, normal or high at 3 AM. Blindly increasing evening insulin worsens Somogyi rebound.
stem: A patient on evening insulin reports morning headaches and night sweats. What is suspected?

options: Give aspirin for the fever
Administer levothyroxine
Cool with an alcohol bath only

Treat as thyroid storm in the ICU with a beta-blocker such as esmolol or propranolol, an antithyroid drug, iodine after the antithyroid drug, steroids, cooling, and treatment of the precipitant; avoid aspirin because it displaces thyroid hormone
rationale: Thyroid storm is life-threatening multi-system decompensation requiring ICU care: beta-blockade for adrenergic symptoms, thionamide to block synthesis, iodine at least an hour later to block release, steroids to prevent T4 to T3 conversion, plus cooling and precipitant treatment. Aspirin increases free thyroid hormone and is avoided.
stem: A 34-year-old with hyperthyroidism, after an illness, has temperature 104F, HR 150, agitation, and nausea, with a high Burch-Wartofsky score. What is the priority?

options: Iodine first, then methimazole
Levothyroxine then iodine
Give the thionamide such as methimazole or PTU first, then iodine at least 1 hour later; iodine given first provides substrate for more hormone synthesis
Beta-blocker only, with no antithyroid drug needed
rationale: The thionamide must block new hormone synthesis before iodine is given, because iodine administered first fuels additional hormone production through the Jod-Basedow effect. Only after synthesis blockade does iodine's inhibition of hormone release become therapeutic.
stem: What is the correct medication sequence in thyroid storm?

options: Strict medication adherence
Infection, surgery, trauma, DKA, or abrupt antithyroid withdrawal; any major stressor can trigger storm in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism
Adequate hydration
Beta-blocker therapy
rationale: Thyroid storm is precipitated by acute physiologic stress in patients with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, so prevention centers on controlling the hyperthyroidism and managing stressors proactively. Adherence, hydration, and beta-blockers are protective, not precipitants.
stem: Which factors can precipitate thyroid storm in a hyperthyroid patient?

options: SIADH, with euvolemic hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine, and high urine sodium; treat the cause, restrict fluids, and consider hypertonic saline if severely symptomatic
Diabetes insipidus
Dehydration; give isotonic fluids
Normal sodium handling
rationale: SIADH causes water retention with dilutional hyponatremia, clinical euvolemia, concentrated urine with osmolality above 100, and urine sodium above 40. Fluids worsen the dilution, so fluid restriction is first-line, with hypertonic saline reserved for severe symptoms.
stem: A 68-year-old with small cell lung cancer has Na 122 mEq/L, concentrated urine, and no edema; he is euvolemic. What is the diagnosis?

options: SIADH
Central diabetes insipidus from ADH deficiency, causing polyuria of dilute urine with hypernatremia and thirst; treat with desmopressin and replace fluids
Psychogenic polydipsia
Normal postoperative diuresis
rationale: Pituitary surgery can injure ADH production, producing massive dilute urine output with hypernatremia and thirst that defines central DI. Desmopressin replaces ADH, and free water is replaced. SIADH would show concentrated urine with hyponatremia, the opposite pattern.
stem: A patient after pituitary surgery has massive dilute urine output of 500 mL/hr, thirst, and Na 152 mEq/L. What is the diagnosis?

options: SIADH causes polyuria, dilute urine, and hypernatremia
DI causes oliguria, concentrated urine, and hyponatremia
Both cause identical findings
SIADH causes oliguria with concentrated urine and hyponatremia, while DI causes polyuria with dilute urine and hypernatremia; they are opposite disorders of ADH
rationale: SIADH is ADH excess causing water retention, while DI is ADH deficiency or resistance causing water loss, so urine output, urine concentration, and serum sodium move in opposite directions. Recognizing the mirror-image pattern prevents dangerous mistreatment such as giving fluids to SIADH.
stem: Which pairing correctly contrasts SIADH and diabetes insipidus?

options: Replace free water orally if able, otherwise with hypotonic IV fluids such as D5W, plus desmopressin; monitor sodium, urine output, and osmolality closely
Restrict fluids
Give hypertonic saline
Give isotonic saline only
rationale: Central DI loses free water, so management replaces water with oral intake or hypotonic fluids plus desmopressin to replace ADH. Close monitoring prevents overly rapid sodium correction. Fluid restriction and hypertonic saline would worsen hypernatremia.
stem: A central DI patient has Na 155 mEq/L and is alert and thirsty. What is the management?

options: The SIADH patient with Na 130, mild headache, stable
The DI patient on desmopressin with Na 142 and stable output
The SIADH patient with Na 114 who is seizing from severe symptomatic hyponatremia
The postoperative patient with Na 138
rationale: A sodium of 114 with seizures is a neurologic emergency regardless of cause and requires hypertonic saline per protocol to raise sodium enough to stop the seizures. Stable patients with mild or normal abnormalities can safely wait.
stem: At the start of the shift, which patient warrants assessment first?

options: Administer his scheduled glipizide now and recheck glucose in 1 hour.
Keep him NPO and start a continuous IV dextrose infusion.
Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck glucose in 15 minutes.
Inject glucagon intramuscularly and activate the rapid response team.
rationale: A conscious patient with hypoglycemia who can swallow safely is treated with the 15-15 rule: 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat until glucose is above 70 mg/dL. Giving more sulfonylurea would deepen hypoglycemia, and glucagon or IV dextrose are reserved for patients who are unconscious, seizing, or unable to swallow safely. Keeping him NPO only delays treatment of a time-sensitive problem.
stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes glipizide each morning. On the medical-surgical unit he skipped lunch and now reports shakiness and sweating. Bedside glucose is 52 mg/dL. He is alert, oriented, and able to swallow. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Begin aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation before starting insulin.
Start a regular insulin infusion immediately to stop ketone production.
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the severe acidosis.
Give IV potassium chloride to prevent insulin-induced hypokalemia.
rationale: DKA causes profound volume depletion, and isotonic fluids restore perfusion, dilute glucose, and improve insulin responsiveness; insulin is started only after initial fluid resuscitation because it drives potassium intracellularly and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse in a hypovolemic patient. Bicarbonate is not indicated for pH above 6.9 and does not address the underlying problem, and potassium is repleted only after confirming adequate renal function and a level below 5.2, not given empirically when it is already elevated.
stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes arrives in the ED with Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath odor, and abdominal pain. Labs: glucose 512 mg/dL, pH 7.21, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, positive serum ketones. Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg and heart rate is 122 bpm. What is the priority initial intervention?

options: Administer the scheduled levothyroxine dose to stabilize thyroid levels.
Prepare the patient for emergent radioactive iodine ablation.
Restrict oral fluids to prevent worsening of the tachycardia.
Administer the prescribed beta-blocker and apply active cooling measures.
rationale: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis, and immediate priorities are blunting the sympathetic surge with a beta-blocker and reducing hyperthermia with cooling, alongside treating the precipitating infection. Giving thyroid hormone would worsen the crisis, radioactive iodine is not an acute intervention, and fluid restriction is inappropriate in a febrile, tachycardic patient who needs volume support.
stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves disease was admitted for pneumonia. On day 2 she develops a temperature of 104.1 F, heart rate 148 bpm, agitation, and nausea. The provider suspects thyroid storm. Which nursing action takes priority?

options: Reassure her that tingling is an expected effect of anesthesia wearing off.
Notify the provider, check the serum calcium, and have IV calcium gluconate available.
Administer her scheduled levothyroxine dose to replace missing thyroid hormone.
Encourage ambulation to improve circulation to the extremities.
rationale: Perioral and fingertip paresthesia with a positive Chvostek sign indicates hypocalcemia from inadvertent parathyroid injury or removal, which can progress to laryngospasm and tetany; the nurse should obtain a calcium level, notify the provider, and have IV calcium gluconate ready. Reassurance and ambulation ignore a potentially airway-threatening electrolyte emergency, and levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone but does nothing for acute hypocalcemia.
stem: A 45-year-old woman is on postoperative day 1 after total thyroidectomy on the surgical stepdown unit. She reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. The nurse notes a positive Chvostek sign. Vital signs are stable. What is the best nursing action?

options: Administer IV regular insulin with glucose to lower the potassium level.
Give oral sodium chloride tablets and encourage oral fluid intake.
Administer IV hydrocortisone with isotonic fluid boluses and dextrose as needed.
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate to treat the hyperkalemia.
rationale: This is adrenal (Addisonian) crisis: abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal causing hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. The life-saving treatment is immediate IV hydrocortisone plus large-volume isotonic fluids and dextrose for hypoglycemia, which corrects the cortisol deficiency driving all of the abnormalities. Insulin or Kayexalate would treat only the potassium number while the patient remains in shock, and oral therapy is inadequate for a hypotensive, vomiting patient.
stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic adrenal insufficiency stopped taking his hydrocortisone three days ago because he felt well. In the ED he has nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, heart rate 118 bpm, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 6.0 mEq/L, and glucose 58 mg/dL. What is the priority treatment?

options: Administer aggressive isotonic IV fluids to restore perfusion and lower osmolality.
Give an IV bolus of regular insulin to rapidly lower the glucose level.
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic derangement.
Restrict IV fluids to avoid precipitating cerebral edema.
rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is defined by extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketoacidosis, and the profound osmotic diuresis causes severe volume depletion; isotonic fluid resuscitation is the first priority because it restores perfusion and alone substantially lowers glucose and osmolality. Insulin is added only after fluids are underway, bicarbonate is unnecessary with a normal pH, and fluid restriction would worsen the hyperosmolar dehydration driving his altered mentation.
stem: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to the ED with several days of polyuria and progressive confusion. Labs: glucose 986 mg/dL, serum osmolality 344 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, trace urine ketones. Blood pressure is 94/60 mmHg. What is the priority initial intervention?

options: Encourage oral fluid intake to dilute the concentrated urine.
Administer hypotonic IV fluids to correct the sodium gradually.
Administer desmopressin to reduce free water excretion.
Enforce the fluid restriction, monitor neurologic status, and maintain seizure precautions.
rationale: In SIADH the body retains free water, producing dilutional hyponatremia, so the cornerstone of management is restricting free water intake while closely watching for worsening neurologic symptoms such as seizures from the severe hyponatremia. Encouraging fluids or giving hypotonic IV fluids would further dilute serum sodium, and desmopressin promotes water retention, which is the opposite of what this patient needs.
stem: A 60-year-old man with small cell lung cancer is admitted to telemetry with headache and confusion. Sodium is 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and urine osmolality is inappropriately high. He is euvolemic with no edema. The provider diagnoses SIADH and orders fluid restriction. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Restrict fluids to prevent worsening of the hypernatremia.
Administer prescribed desmopressin and monitor strict intake and output with sodium trends.
Encourage a high-sodium diet to match the urinary losses.
Administer a loop diuretic to reduce the excessive urine output.
rationale: This is central diabetes insipidus from pituitary injury: absent ADH causes massive dilute diuresis and hypernatremia. Desmopressin replaces ADH to concentrate the urine, while strict intake and output with serial sodium levels guides safe correction. Fluid restriction would worsen hypernatremic dehydration, a high-sodium diet is contraindicated with a sodium of 152, and diuretics would increase free water loss.
stem: A 38-year-old woman is postoperative day 2 after transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary adenoma. She reports intense thirst and is voiding 350 to 400 mL of dilute urine per hour. Labs: sodium 152 mEq/L, serum osmolality 312 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Rewarm her rapidly with heated blankets and warm IV fluids.
Administer a prescribed sedative so she can rest comfortably.
Support airway and breathing, rewarm gently, and prepare for IV levothyroxine and hydrocortisone.
Give her levothyroxine orally with breakfast and recheck vital signs in 4 hours.
rationale: Myxedema coma is a life-threatening decompensation of hypothyroidism with hypoventilation, bradycardia, hypotension, and hypothermia; priorities are airway and breathing support, gentle passive rewarming, and IV thyroid hormone plus stress-dose hydrocortisone because adrenal insufficiency may coexist. Rapid active rewarming can cause cardiovascular collapse, sedatives further depress respirations in these patients, and oral levothyroxine is too slow and unreliable with decreased gut absorption.
stem: A 78-year-old woman with hypothyroidism stopped taking levothyroxine two months ago. She is found lethargic with a temperature of 94.2 F, heart rate 44 bpm, blood pressure 88/58 mmHg, and shallow respirations at 10 per minute. What is the priority nursing action?

options: I will inject air into the NPH vial, then air into the regular vial, and draw up the regular insulin first.
I will draw up the NPH insulin first since it is the larger dose, then add the regular.
I will mix my glargine with regular insulin the same way to save injections.
I will shake both vials vigorously before drawing up the dose.
rationale: The correct sequence is air into cloudy (NPH), air into clear (regular), then draw clear before cloudy, which prevents contaminating the regular insulin vial with NPH and altering its rapid onset. Drawing NPH first risks exactly that contamination, glargine must never be mixed with any other insulin because it changes its pH-dependent absorption, and shaking denatures insulin proteins so vials should only be gently rolled.
stem: A 55-year-old man newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes is learning to mix NPH and regular insulin in one syringe for his morning dose. Which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding of the technique?

options: Continue the insulin infusion and add potassium to the IV fluids.
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to improve insulin effectiveness.
Restrict IV fluids to concentrate the serum potassium.
Hold the insulin infusion and replete potassium before resuming insulin.
rationale: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly, so starting or continuing insulin with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L risks precipitating life-threatening hypokalemia and cardiac arrest; guidelines require holding insulin and repleting potassium until it is above 3.3 mEq/L. Continuing the infusion while adding potassium still exposes the patient to a dangerous intracellular shift, bicarbonate does not fix hypokalemia, and restricting fluids worsens the volume depletion of DKA.
stem: A 29-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is being treated for DKA in the stepdown unit. His latest labs show potassium 3.2 mEq/L, and the insulin infusion is running. He has adequate urine output. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Pour orange juice into his mouth and elevate the head of the bed.
Administer IV dextrose 50% per protocol and recheck glucose in 15 minutes.
Give his scheduled rapid-acting insulin to correct the rebound hyperglycemia.
Place him NPO, turn him to his side, and recheck glucose in 1 hour.
rationale: An unconscious hypoglycemic patient with IV access needs immediate IV dextrose, which raises blood glucose within minutes; oral carbohydrates are an aspiration risk in anyone unable to swallow safely. Giving insulin would be catastrophic, and simply repositioning him while waiting an hour leaves the brain without glucose and risks seizure, coma, or death.
stem: A 55-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive in his hospital bed during night shift. Bedside glucose is 38 mg/dL. He has an IV line in place. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Encourage a high-sodium diet to correct the electrolyte imbalance.
Administer IV insulin with glucose to shift potassium into the cells.
Replace potassium per protocol with continuous cardiac monitoring.
Restrict fluids to prevent dilution of the serum potassium.
rationale: Excess cortisol in Cushing syndrome drives renal potassium wasting, and a level of 2.8 with muscle weakness and U waves places the patient at risk for lethal dysrhythmias, so potassium must be replaced promptly under cardiac monitoring. Insulin with glucose would worsen hypokalemia by shifting potassium intracellularly, sodium loading does not replace potassium, and fluid restriction does nothing to correct total-body potassium depletion.
stem: A 47-year-old woman with Cushing syndrome is admitted to telemetry for evaluation. Morning labs show potassium 2.8 mEq/L, and she reports muscle weakness and cramping. The ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. What is the priority nursing action?

options: I will call my provider right away if I develop a fever or sore throat.
I can stop the medication once my rapid heartbeat goes away.
I should take it on an empty stomach and skip doses if I feel nauseated.
This medication will cause me to lose the weight I gained.
rationale: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, so fever or sore throat are warning signs of a dangerously low neutrophil count and require immediate evaluation. Stopping the drug when symptoms improve leads to relapse of hyperthyroidism, it may be taken with food to reduce GI upset rather than skipped, and hyperthyroidism causes weight loss, so successful treatment typically causes modest weight gain, not loss.
stem: A 29-year-old woman is newly prescribed methimazole for Graves disease. During discharge teaching on the medical-surgical unit, which statement by the patient indicates a correct understanding of the medication?

options: Restrict IV fluids to avoid overloading her postoperative heart.
Administer a prescribed dose of rapid-acting insulin for stress hyperglycemia.
Encourage a high-potassium diet to replace surgical losses.
Notify the provider for additional stress-dose hydrocortisone and give IV fluid boluses.
rationale: After removing a cortisol-secreting adrenal gland, the suppressed remaining gland cannot meet surgical stress demands, producing acute adrenal insufficiency with hypotension, tachycardia, and nausea; she needs additional stress-dose hydrocortisone and isotonic volume resuscitation. Fluid restriction would deepen shock, insulin is not indicated without hyperglycemia, and potassium supplementation is inappropriate because adrenal insufficiency causes hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.
stem: A 52-year-old woman had a unilateral adrenalectomy yesterday for Cushing syndrome. This morning her blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg, heart rate 112 bpm, and she reports nausea and profound fatigue. She received her scheduled hydrocortisone dose. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Take it at bedtime with a small snack to improve absorption.
Take it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, at the same time each day.
Take it together with your calcium and iron supplements for convenience.
Double the dose if you miss a day so your levels stay steady.
rationale: Levothyroxine absorption is significantly reduced by food, so it must be taken on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, consistently at the same time daily to maintain stable levels. Calcium, iron, and soy bind the drug and must be separated by at least 4 hours, bedtime dosing with food impairs absorption, and doubling doses risks precipitating cardiac dysrhythmias.
stem: A 63-year-old man is newly prescribed levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. Which teaching point is most important for the nurse to include?

options: Palpate the abdomen frequently to monitor tumor size changes.
Start a beta-blocker immediately to control his heart rate before alpha blockade is complete.
Ensure adequate alpha blockade is established before any beta-blocker is given, and avoid abdominal palpation.
Restrict fluids to prevent hypertensive episodes from volume overload.
rationale: Alpha-adrenergic blockade must be established before beta-blockade because unopposed alpha stimulation from beta-blockade alone can trigger a catastrophic hypertensive crisis, and abdominal palpation can mechanically trigger catecholamine release from the tumor. Frequent palpation risks provoking a crisis, beta-blockers given first are dangerous, and these patients are typically volume-depleted and need hydration, not restriction.
stem: A 41-year-old man with a pheochromocytoma is scheduled for adrenalectomy in two weeks. He is started on phenoxybenzamine. Which nursing action is the priority during the preoperative period?

options: Administer subcutaneous basal insulin and overlap it 1 to 2 hours before stopping the infusion.
Stop the insulin infusion now since the glucose is below 200 mg/dL.
Continue the infusion until discharge to prevent relapse of ketoacidosis.
Switch to sliding-scale regular insulin only, with no basal insulin.
rationale: DKA is resolved when the anion gap closes, bicarbonate normalizes, and pH corrects, all of which have occurred here; to prevent rebound ketoacidosis, subcutaneous basal insulin must be given 1 to 2 hours before the infusion stops because IV insulin clears within minutes. Stopping the drip without overlap leaves the patient with no insulin, continuing it after resolution is unnecessary, and sliding scale alone provides no basal coverage for a type 1 diabetic.
stem: A 33-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has been on an insulin infusion for DKA for 18 hours. Current labs: glucose 178 mg/dL, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, pH 7.36, anion gap 10, and she is eating a regular diet. What is the correct next step?

options: Discharge her once her glucose is above 70 mg/dL after one more snack.
Administer her evening glyburide dose to prevent rebound hyperglycemia.
Restrict her carbohydrate intake to stabilize glucose levels.
Anticipate prolonged monitoring with dextrose support, as sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia can recur for 24 to 72 hours.
rationale: Glyburide is long-acting and renally cleared, so in an elderly patient with kidney disease its hypoglycemic effect persists for 24 to 72 hours with a high risk of recurrent episodes; she needs admission, dextrose infusion or repeated glucose monitoring, and the sulfonylurea held. A single snack does not outlast the drug, giving more glyburide would worsen hypoglycemia, and carbohydrate restriction is counterproductive during active hypoglycemia.
stem: An 82-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease takes glyburide daily. She is admitted after a hypoglycemic episode at home that resolved with juice, but 6 hours later her glucose is 48 mg/dL again despite eating lunch. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Remove the dressing to inspect the incision and estimate blood loss.
Keep the patient NPO and offer ice chips to soothe the throat.
Administer IV calcium gluconate for suspected hypocalcemia.
Call the surgeon immediately, keep the patient upright, and have the tracheostomy tray at the bedside.
rationale: Neck swelling with stridor after thyroidectomy signals postoperative hemorrhage compressing the airway, which is an immediate airway emergency; the surgeon must be called stat while keeping the patient upright with emergency airway equipment ready, since the hematoma may need bedside evacuation. Removing the dressing can release tamponade and worsen bleeding, ice chips risk aspiration with a compromised airway, and calcium treats hypocalcemia, not hemorrhage.
stem: A 50-year-old man is 6 hours post-total thyroidectomy on the surgical unit. The nurse notes increasing neck swelling, a saturated pressure dressing, and the patient develops stridor with a respiratory rate of 28 per minute. What is the priority nursing action?

options: A small garden salad with fat-free dressing and diet soda.
A low-calorie, high-fiber meal to control her rapid metabolism.
A high-calorie, high-protein meal such as chicken, rice, eggs, and whole milk.
A high-sugar meal with candy and sweetened beverages for quick energy.
rationale: Hyperthyroidism creates a hypermetabolic state with increased caloric and protein needs plus negative nitrogen balance, so patients require high-calorie, high-protein meals to prevent further weight and muscle loss. Low-calorie or salad-only meals worsen the catabolic deficit, and concentrated sweets cause rapid glucose swings without providing the sustained protein and calories needed.
stem: A 36-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hyperthyroidism asks the nurse what she should eat. She has lost 12 pounds in two months despite a good appetite. Which meal selection indicates correct understanding of her nutritional needs?

options: I will double or triple my hydrocortisone during illness or fever, wear a medical alert bracelet, and never stop it abruptly.
I can skip my hydrocortisone on days I feel well to give my adrenals a rest.
I should follow a strict low-sodium diet to protect my blood pressure.
I only need to take the medication until my energy returns, then I can stop.
rationale: Addison disease requires lifelong glucocorticoid replacement with stress-dose increases during illness, fever, or surgery because the adrenals cannot mount a cortisol response, plus a medical alert bracelet since abrupt withdrawal can precipitate fatal crisis. Skipping doses or stopping when feeling better invites adrenal crisis, and these patients lose sodium and need adequate salt intake, not sodium restriction.
stem: A 44-year-old man newly diagnosed with Addison disease is being discharged on daily hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding of long-term management?

options: A 22-year-old with glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.22, and large serum ketones.
A 35-year-old with glucose 520 mg/dL, Kussmaul respirations, and fruity breath.
A 28-year-old with glucose 450 mg/dL, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and vomiting.
A 74-year-old with glucose 1,120 mg/dL, serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38, and trace ketones.
rationale: HHS is distinguished by extreme hyperglycemia, marked hyperosmolality above 320, minimal or absent ketosis, and a normal pH, typically in older type 2 diabetics with profound dehydration and altered mentation. The other three presentations show significant ketoacidosis with low pH, low bicarbonate, and large ketones, which defines DKA rather than HHS.
stem: The ED nurse is triaging four patients with hyperglycemia. Which patient presentation is most consistent with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state rather than diabetic ketoacidosis?

options: Hold all insulin while he is NPO to prevent hypoglycemia during surgery.
Continue his basal insulin at the usual dose and hold the mealtime bolus doses.
Give only sliding-scale regular insulin every 6 hours while NPO.
Switch him to his oral diabetes medication the morning of surgery.
rationale: A type 1 diabetic always needs basal insulin even when NPO because the body continuously requires background insulin to prevent ketoacidosis, while mealtime boluses are held without food intake. Holding all insulin risks DKA, sliding scale alone provides no basal coverage and is reactive rather than physiologic, and oral agents are inappropriate for type 1 diabetes and most perioperative management.
stem: A 48-year-old man with type 1 diabetes uses basal-bolus insulin and is NPO after midnight for morning surgery on the surgical unit. His bedtime glucose was 142 mg/dL. What is the correct insulin plan?

options: Administer IV insulin with glucose to drive potassium into the cells.
Replace potassium per protocol under continuous cardiac monitoring.
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate to bind intestinal potassium.
Encourage vigorous exercise to promote potassium uptake by muscles.
rationale: A potassium of 2.9 with U waves and muscle weakness signals dangerous total-body depletion that predisposes to lethal ventricular dysrhythmias, so repletion under cardiac monitoring is the priority. Insulin with glucose would shift even more potassium intracellularly and worsen the deficit, Kayexalate removes potassium and is contraindicated, and exercise cannot correct severe hypokalemia.
stem: A 58-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism is admitted to telemetry with hypertension and muscle cramps. Labs show potassium 2.9 mEq/L, and the ECG shows flattened T waves with prominent U waves. He reports leg weakness. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Delay insulin therapy until after delivery to avoid fetal hypoglycemia.
Give oral fluids and oral potassium to correct the deficit gradually.
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to rapidly normalize the maternal pH.
Begin aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with continuous maternal and fetal monitoring.
rationale: DKA in pregnancy threatens both mother and fetus because ketoacidosis reduces uteroplacental perfusion, so aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation with standard DKA insulin management plus continuous fetal monitoring is required without delay. Delaying treatment endangers both patients, oral rehydration is inadequate for severe DKA with vomiting, and bicarbonate is not indicated for pH above 6.9.
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation with type 1 diabetes presents to labor and delivery with vomiting and abdominal pain. Labs: glucose 420 mg/dL, pH 7.24, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, positive ketones. Fetal heart tracing is category II. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Avoid close contact with others, flush the toilet twice after use, and use separate laundry for several days.
No special precautions are needed because the radiation dose is too small to matter.
Stop taking antithyroid medication permanently the day before treatment.
Resume normal contact with pregnant family members immediately after discharge.
rationale: Radioactive iodine emits radiation in sweat, saliva, and urine for several days, so patients must limit close contact, practice meticulous toilet hygiene, and launder clothing separately to protect household members. Precautions are definitely required, antithyroid medications are typically held before therapy rather than stopped permanently without orders, and contact with pregnant women and children must be avoided for the prescribed period.
stem: A 40-year-old woman with Graves disease is scheduled for radioactive iodine therapy next week. During teaching in the clinic, which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding of radiation precautions?

options: Elevated sodium, decreased potassium, and elevated glucose.
Elevated calcium, decreased phosphate, and metabolic alkalosis.
Low sodium, elevated potassium, and low glucose.
Elevated sodium, elevated potassium, and elevated glucose.
rationale: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes loss of aldosterone and cortisol, producing renal sodium wasting with hyponatremia, impaired potassium excretion with hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia from cortisol deficiency. The other combinations describe different disorders: elevated sodium with low potassium suggests hyperaldosteronism or Cushing syndrome, and elevated glucose is typical of Cushing syndrome, not Addison disease.
stem: A 39-year-old man with known Addison disease is admitted with fatigue, dizziness, salt craving, and bronze hyperpigmentation of his skin creases. Which laboratory pattern does the nurse expect to find?

options: Increase his bedtime long-acting insulin to bring down the morning glucose.
Check his blood glucose at 2 to 3 AM for several nights to differentiate the cause.
Skip breakfast to prevent the morning glucose from rising further.
Switch his morning insulin to the evening to cover the dawn hours.
rationale: Nocturnal hypoglycemia with rebound morning hyperglycemia (Somogyi effect) is distinguished from the dawn phenomenon by checking a 2 to 3 AM glucose: low suggests Somogyi, normal or high suggests dawn phenomenon. Increasing bedtime insulin would worsen Somogyi-related hypoglycemia, skipping breakfast does not address the overnight pattern, and moving insulin without data risks further hypoglycemia.
stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes bedtime glargine and reports fasting glucose readings of 220 to 250 mg/dL despite good daytime control. His provider wants to determine whether this is the Somogyi effect or the dawn phenomenon. What should the nurse instruct him to do?

options: Mix it with rapid-acting insulin in the same syringe to reduce injections.
Expect a strong peak effect 4 to 6 hours after injection.
Refrigerate the open pen between uses and discard after 90 days.
Take it once daily at the same time, never mix it with other insulins, and discard the open vial after 28 days.
rationale: Glargine is a peakless basal insulin designed for once-daily dosing at a consistent time, and it must never be mixed with other insulins because mixing alters its pH-dependent prolonged absorption. It does not have a pronounced peak like NPH, and once opened it is kept at room temperature and discarded after 28 days rather than refrigerated for 90 days.
stem: A 61-year-old man is newly prescribed insulin glargine at bedtime for type 2 diabetes. Which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding of this insulin?

options: Anticipate that he needs lower insulin doses and monitor closely for hypoglycemia.
Increase his insulin doses because uremia causes insulin resistance.
Hold all insulin since his kidneys can no longer clear it safely.
Switch him to a sulfonylurea because it is safer in kidney disease.
rationale: The kidneys clear insulin, so as renal function declines insulin lingers longer and requirements fall, creating a high risk of hypoglycemia if doses are not reduced. Increasing doses would provoke severe hypoglycemia, holding all insulin in a type 1 diabetic invites ketoacidosis, and sulfonylureas are dangerous in CKD because reduced clearance prolongs their hypoglycemic effect.
stem: A 66-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease is admitted to the medical-surgical unit with a urinary tract infection. His creatinine has risen from 2.8 to 3.6 mg/dL. He takes basal-bolus insulin at home. What should the nurse anticipate regarding his insulin needs?

options: Give the iodine preparation first to block hormone release, then the antithyroid drug.
Administer the antithyroid drug and the iodine preparation at the exact same time.
Give the antithyroid drug first, then administer iodine at least 1 hour later.
Give levothyroxine first to protect the thyroid gland from the iodine.
rationale: In thyroid storm, the antithyroid drug (propylthiouracil or methimazole) must be given first to block new hormone synthesis, and iodine is administered at least 1 hour later to block release of preformed hormone; giving iodine first would provide raw material for even more thyroid hormone production. Levothyroxine would add fuel to the hyperthyroid crisis and is never given.
stem: A 44-year-old woman with Graves disease is in thyroid storm in the ICU. The provider orders propylthiouracil, saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI), a beta-blocker, and hydrocortisone. In which order should the nurse administer the propylthiouracil and the SSKI?

options: Mild headache controlled with acetaminophen.
Clear, watery drainage from the nose that tests positive for glucose.
Mild nasal congestion from the surgical packing.
Nausea that resolves within a few hours of surgery.
rationale: Clear watery rhinorrhea after transsphenoidal surgery suggests a cerebrospinal fluid leak, which creates a direct pathway for meningitis and requires immediate provider notification with precautions such as avoiding nose blowing and straining. Mild headache, expected congestion from packing, and transient nausea are common postoperative findings that do not indicate a CSF leak.
stem: A 49-year-old woman is postoperative day 1 after transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary tumor. Which finding should the nurse report to the surgeon immediately?

options: Restrict oral fluids to prevent worsening of the hypercalcemia.
Administer a thiazide diuretic to promote calcium excretion.
Encourage bedrest to protect weakened bones from fracture.
Administer vigorous isotonic IV fluids and encourage mobilization.
rationale: Hypercalcemia causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration, so aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation restores renal perfusion and promotes urinary calcium excretion, while mobilization prevents further bone resorption from immobility. Fluid restriction worsens the dehydration driving the crisis, thiazides increase calcium reabsorption and are contraindicated, and bedrest accelerates bone calcium release.
stem: A 62-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism presents with confusion, constipation, polyuria, and muscle weakness. Calcium is 13.1 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg with dry mucous membranes. What is the priority nursing intervention?

options: I will rotate injection sites, use my abdomen for the most consistent absorption, and not massage the site.
I will use the same spot on my thigh every time so absorption stays predictable.
I will inject through my clothing when I am in a hurry to save time.
I will draw the insulin into the syringe an hour early so it warms up.
rationale: Rotating sites prevents lipohypertrophy that impairs absorption, the abdomen provides the most rapid and consistent absorption, and massaging the site speeds absorption unpredictably and should be avoided. Repeatedly using one spot causes tissue damage and erratic absorption, injecting through clothing risks contamination and inaccurate dosing, and insulin should be at room temperature but not drawn excessively early.
stem: A 35-year-old woman newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes is learning subcutaneous insulin injection technique. Which statement indicates correct understanding?

options: Increase the IV fluid rate to correct the dehydration more quickly.
Administer IV mannitol prophylactically to prevent brain swelling.
Slow the rate of osmolarity correction, perform frequent neurologic checks, and notify the provider.
Give a bolus of regular insulin to lower glucose faster.
rationale: Headache, altered mentation, and pupillary changes during DKA treatment suggest cerebral edema, a medical emergency treated by slowing fluid and osmolarity correction, elevating the head of the bed, and obtaining emergent neuroimaging and mannitol or hypertonic saline per orders. Increasing fluids or pushing insulin faster worsens the osmotic shifts driving brain swelling, and prophylactic mannitol is not given without signs of herniation.
stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is 6 hours into DKA treatment with IV fluids and an insulin infusion. He now complains of a severe headache, becomes increasingly drowsy, and his pupils are sluggish. Blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Administer IV insulin with glucose to lower the potassium quickly.
Administer IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluids, with calcium if QRS widening develops.
Restrict dietary potassium and recheck the level in the morning.
Administer spironolactone to promote renal potassium excretion.
rationale: Hyperkalemia in adrenal insufficiency results from aldosterone deficiency, so definitive treatment is glucocorticoid replacement with isotonic fluids, which restores renal potassium excretion; IV calcium is added if ECG changes progress to protect the myocardium. Insulin with glucose only temporarily shifts potassium and ignores the underlying cortisol deficiency, morning rechecks are too slow for a potassium of 6.2 with ECG changes, and spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that would worsen hyperkalemia.
stem: A 56-year-old woman with Addison disease missed several hydrocortisone doses during a gastrointestinal illness. Labs show potassium 6.2 mEq/L with peaked T waves on the ECG. Blood pressure is 90/58 mmHg. What is the priority treatment?

options: Stop taking insulin while you are not eating to avoid low blood sugar.
Skip glucose checks since you are not eating regular meals.
Take an extra dose of glyburide to make up for missed meals.
Never stop your basal insulin, check glucose and ketones frequently, stay hydrated, and seek care for vomiting or moderate to large ketones.
rationale: During illness, counterregulatory hormones raise glucose and ketone production, so basal insulin must never be stopped even without food intake; frequent monitoring for ketones and dehydration with clear thresholds for seeking care prevents DKA. Stopping insulin invites ketoacidosis, skipping checks blinds the patient to dangerous trends, and extra sulfonylurea risks hypoglycemia without food.
stem: A 30-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes calls the clinic because she has influenza, nausea, and has barely eaten for two days. Which sick-day teaching is most important for the nurse to reinforce?

options: Question the sedative order because sedatives can cause dangerous respiratory depression in severe hypothyroidism.
Administer the sedative as ordered since rest will help her recover.
Give the sedative with a full glass of water to speed absorption.
Request a larger sedative dose because hypothyroid patients metabolize drugs faster.
rationale: Severe hypothyroidism slows drug metabolism and depresses respiratory drive, so sedatives and narcotics can precipitate hypoventilation, CO2 retention, and myxedema coma; the nurse should question the order and suggest non-sedating alternatives. Hypothyroid patients metabolize drugs more slowly, not faster, and giving the sedative as ordered puts the patient at serious risk.
stem: A 74-year-old woman with untreated hypothyroidism is admitted with fatigue, bradycardia, and hypothermia. The provider orders a sedative to help her sleep. What is the best nursing action?

options: Wear an eye patch over both eyes to rest the eye muscles.
Rub the eyes frequently to relieve the gritty sensation.
Protect the eyes with sunglasses, use artificial tears, elevate the head of the bed, and report any vision changes.
Avoid all follow-up eye appointments once the bulging improves.
rationale: Graves ophthalmopathy causes proptosis with corneal exposure, so protection with sunglasses, lubrication with artificial tears, head elevation to reduce periorbital edema, and prompt reporting of vision changes or diplopia are essential. Eye patches impair vision and are not indicated, rubbing damages the exposed cornea, and ongoing ophthalmology follow-up is needed because the eye disease can progress independently of thyroid levels.
stem: A 42-year-old woman with Graves disease has periorbital edema, proptosis, and complains of gritty, dry eyes with occasional double vision. Which teaching is most important?

options: Stop the insulin infusion now that glucose is below 250 mg/dL.
Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion until the anion gap closes.
Switch to hypotonic fluids only and discontinue insulin.
Give oral glucose tablets to raise the glucose back above 250 mg/dL.
rationale: When glucose falls to 200 to 250 but the anion gap remains open, dextrose is added to the IV fluids so insulin can be continued to clear the ketoacidosis without causing hypoglycemia. Stopping insulin before the gap closes allows ketoacidosis to recur, hypotonic fluids alone do not treat ketosis, and oral glucose is unreliable in a nauseated DKA patient and does not replace the insulin needed.
stem: A 27-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is being treated for DKA. Current labs: glucose 218 mg/dL, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, anion gap 18, pH 7.28. He is alert and tolerating sips of water. What is the correct next step?

options: Bronze hyperpigmentation of the skin and salt craving.
Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia.
Hypertension with truncal obesity and purple striae.
Pale skin without hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, and low ACTH.
rationale: Secondary adrenal insufficiency stems from pituitary ACTH deficiency, so there is no excess ACTH to cause hyperpigmentation, and aldosterone (regulated mainly by the renin-angiotensin system) is preserved, producing hyponatremia without the severe hyperkalemia of primary disease. Bronze hyperpigmentation marks primary Addison disease, hypernatremia with hypokalemia suggests mineralocorticoid excess, and truncal obesity with striae describes Cushing syndrome.
stem: A 51-year-old man develops fatigue, weight loss, and hypotension months after pituitary surgery. Labs show low cortisol with low ACTH. Which clinical picture best fits secondary adrenal insufficiency rather than primary Addison disease?

options: Hold the lispro dose until the meal tray arrives, then administer it.
Give the lispro now so it has time to start working before the food comes.
Give NPH insulin instead since the meal is delayed.
Double the lispro dose when the tray arrives to cover the delay.
rationale: Rapid-acting lispro peaks within 1 to 2 hours, so giving it without food on the way risks severe hypoglycemia; the dose should be held until the tray arrives and then given with the meal. Giving it early, substituting NPH, or doubling the dose all create dangerous mismatches between insulin action and carbohydrate intake.
stem: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is prescribed insulin lispro with meals on the medical-surgical unit. At noon the nurse is ready to give the dose, but the meal tray is delayed by at least 45 minutes. His pre-meal glucose is 168 mg/dL. What is the best nursing action?

options: Expect a high fever with any infection because cortisol enhances the immune response.
Ignore mild temperature elevations since they are common with Cushing syndrome.
Monitor for subtle signs of infection such as slight temperature elevation or rising WBC, since excess cortisol masks classic signs.
Discontinue hydrocortisone replacement to allow the fever to develop.
rationale: Excess cortisol suppresses the inflammatory response, so infections in Cushing syndrome may present without high fever or obvious signs; the nurse must watch for subtle changes like low-grade temperature elevation, rising WBC, or hyperglycemia. Expecting a high fever misses these blunted presentations, ignoring mild elevations is unsafe, and stopping replacement steroids would precipitate adrenal crisis.
stem: A 46-year-old woman with Cushing syndrome is postoperative day 3 after adrenalectomy and is on hydrocortisone replacement. Her temperature is 100.4 F and WBC is 13,200. She reports the incision looks slightly red. What is the priority nursing interpretation?

options: Restrict all oral fluids until the sodium normalizes.
Encourage a high-salt diet to replace urinary sodium losses.
Replace urinary losses milliliter for milliliter with hypotonic fluids, monitor strict intake and output, and trend sodium and osmolality.
Administer desmopressin to all patients with polyuria regardless of cause.
rationale: Central diabetes insipidus causes massive free water loss, so management centers on replacing urine output to prevent hypernatremic dehydration while trending sodium and osmolality to guide therapy and avoid overly rapid correction. Fluid restriction worsens hypernatremia, a high-salt diet is contraindicated with elevated sodium, and desmopressin is specific to central DI, not to all polyuria.
stem: A 33-year-old man with central diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery is putting out 300 to 450 mL of dilute urine per hour. Sodium is 150 mEq/L and rising. He is alert with intact thirst. What is the priority nursing management?

options: Encourage vigorous aerobic exercise to strengthen the heart muscle.
Administer a prescribed decongestant to reduce cardiac workload.
Reassure him that palpitations are harmless in hyperthyroidism.
Assess the apical pulse, maintain continuous cardiac monitoring, and anticipate beta-blocker therapy.
rationale: Hyperthyroidism increases beta-adrenergic sensitivity and cardiac oxygen demand, predisposing to atrial fibrillation and high-output heart failure, so continuous cardiac monitoring with rate control via beta-blockers is the priority. Vigorous exercise further stresses the hyperdynamic heart, decongestants with sympathomimetics worsen tachycardia, and palpitations in this setting may herald a dangerous dysrhythmia rather than a benign symptom.
stem: A 57-year-old man with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism is admitted to telemetry with a heart rate of 132 bpm, irregular rhythm, and complaints of palpitations. Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Withhold metformin before the contrast study per protocol and report muscle pain, severe fatigue, or rapid breathing.
Double the metformin dose the day before to keep glucose tightly controlled.
Take metformin on an empty stomach the morning of the procedure.
There is no need to adjust metformin because it does not affect the kidneys.
rationale: Iodinated contrast can precipitate acute kidney injury, and metformin accumulation in renal impairment risks lactic acidosis, so it is withheld around contrast administration in at-risk patients, with education about lactic acidosis warning signs. Doubling the dose increases risk, taking it on an empty stomach worsens GI upset without benefit, and metformin is renally cleared, making kidney function directly relevant.
stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily and is scheduled for a CT scan with IV contrast tomorrow. His eGFR is 42 mL/min. What is the most important nursing instruction?

options: Administer oral hydrocortisone and encourage oral fluids.
Give IV regular insulin to correct the hyperkalemia.
Establish large-bore IV access and begin an isotonic fluid bolus immediately.
Restrict sodium intake to prevent worsening hypertension.
rationale: Adrenal crisis presents as hypovolemic shock from cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, so the immediate life-saving action is rapid isotonic volume resuscitation through large-bore access, followed promptly by IV hydrocortisone and dextrose. Oral therapy is inadequate in a hypotensive vomiting patient, insulin treats only one lab value while shock progresses, and sodium restriction is the opposite of what a salt-wasting crisis requires.
stem: A 48-year-old woman with known Addison disease presents to the ED with vomiting, confusion, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, heart rate 124 bpm, sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, and glucose 62 mg/dL after missing doses during a flu illness. What is the first nursing action?

options: Stop the metoprolol immediately because it is causing the diabetes.
Teach him that beta-blockers can mask shakiness and sweating, so he should watch for confusion or unusual behavior and check glucose more often.
Reassure him that beta-blockers prevent hypoglycemia from occurring.
Switch his diabetes medication to insulin to avoid interactions.
rationale: Beta-blockers blunt the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor, palpitations, and sweating, leaving only neuroglycopenic symptoms like confusion, so patients need more frequent glucose monitoring and education about these subtler signs. Stopping metoprolol abruptly risks rebound cardiac events, beta-blockers do not prevent hypoglycemia, and switching diabetes regimens is a provider decision not driven by this interaction.
stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metoprolol for hypertension and glyburide for diabetes. He reports episodes of sudden confusion and clumsiness without the shakiness and sweating he used to feel when his sugar dropped. What is the most important teaching point?

options: Blood glucose below 200 mg/dL on two consecutive checks.
Serum potassium within normal range without supplementation.
Resolution of polyuria and return of normal thirst.
Closed anion gap, bicarbonate 18 or higher, and pH above 7.30.
rationale: DKA resolution is defined by correction of the metabolic acidosis: a closed anion gap, bicarbonate at or above 18, and pH above 7.30, often with glucose already below 200. Glucose alone is misleading because it normalizes before ketosis clears, potassium normalizes with treatment but does not define resolution, and symptom improvement is subjective and lags behind metabolic correction.
stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has been treated for DKA for 14 hours with IV fluids and an insulin infusion. Which laboratory finding best indicates that the ketoacidosis has resolved?

options: Ask the patient to speak and note any hoarseness or weak voice, keeping emergency airway equipment nearby.
Check pedal pulses and capillary refill in both feet.
Offer ice chips immediately to soothe the throat and test swallowing.
Encourage coughing and deep breathing every hour.
rationale: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroidectomy causes vocal cord dysfunction, so the nurse assesses voice quality for hoarseness and keeps airway equipment accessible because bilateral injury can obstruct the airway. Pedal pulses are unrelated to neck surgery, ice chips risk aspiration if vocal cord function is impaired, and vigorous coughing strains the fresh neck incision.
stem: A 54-year-old man is 4 hours post-total thyroidectomy on the surgical stepdown unit. His voice sounds hoarse when he answers questions. Vital signs are stable and there is no stridor. What is the priority nursing assessment and action?

options: A high-sodium, low-potassium, high-sugar diet to match cortisol effects.
A low-protein diet to reduce the workload on the kidneys.
A low-sodium, high-potassium, high-protein, low-concentrated-sugar diet.
An unrestricted diet since Cushing syndrome does not affect nutrition.
rationale: Cushing syndrome causes sodium and water retention, potassium wasting, protein catabolism, and hyperglycemia, so the diet should restrict sodium, replace potassium, provide protein to counter muscle wasting, and limit concentrated sugars. A high-sodium, low-potassium diet would worsen hypertension and hypokalemia, low protein accelerates muscle loss, and ignoring nutrition misses a major modifiable risk.
stem: A 50-year-old woman newly diagnosed with Cushing syndrome asks about diet. She has hypertension, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, elevated glucose, and proximal muscle weakness. Which diet should the nurse recommend?

options: Weigh yourself weekly and report only major changes.
Take orthostatic blood pressures, weigh daily, rise slowly, increase salt and fluid intake as directed, and report dizziness or weight loss.
Follow a strict low-sodium diet and restrict fluids to 1 liter per day.
Stop fludrocortisone on days your blood pressure seems normal.
rationale: Addison disease causes orthostatic hypotension and salt wasting, so daily weights, orthostatic vitals, slow position changes, and adequate salt and fluid intake detect volume depletion early, with dizziness or weight loss signaling the need for evaluation. Weekly weights are too infrequent, sodium and fluid restriction would worsen hypotension, and stopping fludrocortisone invites crisis.
stem: A 37-year-old woman with Addison disease is being discharged on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Which self-management teaching is most important?

options: Freeze unopened vials to extend their expiration date.
Keep the in-use vial in a hot car so it stays at body temperature.
Store all insulin at room temperature indefinitely once purchased.
Refrigerate unopened insulin, keep the in-use vial at room temperature, never freeze it, and discard it after 28 days.
rationale: Unopened insulin is refrigerated to preserve potency, the in-use vial may be kept at room temperature for up to 28 days for comfort and convenience, and freezing or excessive heat denatures the protein and destroys effectiveness. Freezing, heat exposure, and indefinite room-temperature storage all degrade insulin and lead to unpredictable glucose control.
stem: A 28-year-old man newly started on insulin asks how to store it at home. Which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding?

options: Take the antithyroid medication exactly as prescribed without stopping abruptly, and treat infections promptly.
Stop the antithyroid drug whenever you feel well to avoid side effects.
Avoid all medical care for fevers since they are expected with hyperthyroidism.
Increase iodine supplement intake to calm the thyroid gland.
rationale: Thyroid storm is often precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of antithyroid medication, infection, or surgery, so adherence and prompt treatment of infections are the key preventive measures. Stopping the drug invites rebound hyperthyroidism, fevers require evaluation as potential storm triggers, and excess iodine can worsen hyperthyroidism rather than calm it.
stem: A 33-year-old woman with Graves disease on methimazole asks how to prevent thyroid storm. What is the most important teaching point?

options: Increase the empagliflozin dose to improve glucose control during illness.
Check for ketones despite the normal glucose, hold the empagliflozin, and notify the provider.
Reassure her that DKA cannot occur with a glucose below 250 mg/dL.
Give her scheduled empagliflozin and encourage sugary fluids.
rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate euglycemic DKA, in which ketoacidosis develops with glucose below 250, so nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain in this setting demand ketone testing and holding the drug. Increasing the dose worsens the risk, the teaching that DKA requires marked hyperglycemia is dangerously outdated for these agents, and sugary fluids do not address the ketoacidosis.
stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes empagliflozin. She presents to the ED with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after a stomach virus. Glucose is 196 mg/dL, but serum ketones are large and bicarbonate is 14 mEq/L. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Deflate the cuff immediately and document a normal finding.
Keep the cuff inflated, note the carpal spasm as a positive Trousseau sign, and notify the provider to check calcium.
Remove the cuff and apply it to the opposite arm to confirm.
Encourage the patient to relax her hand to stop the spasm.
rationale: Carpal spasm with blood pressure cuff inflation is a positive Trousseau sign indicating neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcemia, a known risk after thyroidectomy from parathyroid injury; the provider needs a calcium level and possible IV calcium replacement. Documenting it as normal, switching arms, or asking the patient to relax all miss a clinically significant finding that can progress to laryngospasm.
stem: A 47-year-old woman is postoperative day 1 after total thyroidectomy. While the nurse takes her blood pressure, her hand develops a painful carpal spasm with the cuff inflated. What is the best nursing action?

options: I check my feet every day, including between my toes.
I wear well-fitting shoes and never walk barefoot.
I keep my blood sugar controlled and see the podiatrist regularly.
I soak my feet in hot water every day to soften the calluses.
rationale: Daily foot inspection, protective footwear, and never walking barefoot are correct diabetic foot practices, but soaking feet in hot water macerates skin, risks burns in neuropathic feet, and promotes breakdown rather than preventing it. Calluses should be managed by a podiatrist, not softened with soaking, which increases ulcer risk.
stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, and a healed foot ulcer is receiving discharge teaching. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options: Avoid abdominal palpation, emotional stress, and stimulant medications, and monitor for hypertensive crisis requiring rapid-acting vasodilators.
Encourage deep abdominal massage to reduce tumor-related pain.
Palpate the abdomen daily to track changes in blood pressure.
Restrict all physical activity until after the tumor is removed.
rationale: Pheochromocytoma releases catecholamines in surges, and mechanical pressure, stress, or stimulants can trigger a life-threatening hypertensive crisis managed with rapid vasodilators such as phentolamine or nitroprusside. Abdominal palpation and massage risk provoking massive catecholamine release, and complete activity restriction is unnecessary with proper alpha blockade.
stem: A 45-year-old man awaiting adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma is on the medical-surgical unit. His blood pressure fluctuates between 150/95 and 210/120 mmHg. Which nursing action is the priority?

options: Both conditions are treated identically with fluid restriction.
The key difference is volume status: SIADH patients are euvolemic or hypervolemic, while cerebral salt wasting patients are hypovolemic and need fluids and salt.
Cerebral salt wasting is treated with fluid restriction just like SIADH.
Sodium levels cannot distinguish the two conditions, so treatment is the same.
rationale: Both SIADH and cerebral salt wasting cause hyponatremia, but SIADH is a euvolemic or hypervolemic state treated with fluid restriction, whereas cerebral salt wasting involves true renal sodium and volume loss requiring isotonic fluids and salt replacement; confusing them and restricting fluids in salt wasting worsens hypovolemia and cerebral perfusion. Volume assessment through orthostatics, mucous membranes, and daily weights is therefore the critical differentiator.
stem: A 55-year-old man with a subarachnoid hemorrhage develops sodium 122 mEq/L. The team is debating SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting. He has dry mucous membranes, orthostatic hypotension, and poor skin turgor. Which interpretation should guide nursing management?

options: Give it by mouth mixed with juice when he becomes confused.
Teach the family to inject it intramuscularly or subcutaneously if he cannot swallow, place him on his side, and call emergency services.
Administer it intravenously for the fastest effect at home.
Use it only after calling the provider for permission during the episode.
rationale: Glucagon is given intramuscularly or subcutaneously by family when the patient cannot safely swallow, the side-lying position protects the airway if vomiting occurs, and emergency services should be called because glucagon is a bridge, not definitive care. Oral administration is an aspiration risk in an impaired patient, home IV use is not feasible, and waiting for provider permission during severe hypoglycemia wastes critical time.
stem: A 40-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has recurrent severe hypoglycemia. His wife asks how to use the emergency glucagon kit at home. What is the most important teaching?

options: Give the SSKI first to quickly block hormone release, then the methimazole.
Give both medications simultaneously to save time.
Give levothyroxine along with the SSKI to protect the gland.
Give methimazole first, then give the SSKI at least 1 hour later.
rationale: The antithyroid drug must be administered first to block synthesis of new thyroid hormone, and iodine given at least 1 hour later blocks release of stored hormone; reversing the order gives the gland more substrate to make additional hormone and worsens the storm. Simultaneous administration still risks iodine being used for new synthesis, and levothyroxine would add hormone to an already thyrotoxic patient.
stem: A 39-year-old woman in thyroid storm has orders for methimazole and saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI). Which administration sequence is correct?

options: Give stress-dose hydrocortisone before, during, and after surgery as ordered, and never hold steroids perioperatively.
Hold all hydrocortisone on the morning of surgery to let the adrenals recover.
Stop fludrocortisone permanently since surgery cures Addison disease.
No steroid changes are needed for minor procedures.
rationale: Surgical stress dramatically increases cortisol requirements that Addison patients cannot meet endogenously, so stress-dose hydrocortisone is given perioperatively and steroids are never held, since abrupt withdrawal precipitates adrenal crisis. Holding doses or stopping fludrocortisone risks intraoperative cardiovascular collapse, and even minor procedures require stress dosing.
stem: A 50-year-old man with Addison disease is scheduled for an elective hernia repair. He takes hydrocortisone 20 mg daily and fludrocortisone. What is the correct perioperative plan?

options: Use sliding-scale regular insulin alone, since it is simpler and safer.
Hold all insulin while the patient is NPO to avoid hypoglycemia.
Use a basal-bolus regimen with basal insulin continued and nutritional insulin adjusted to intake.
Give only long-acting insulin once daily with no mealtime coverage.
rationale: Basal-bolus insulin mimics physiologic secretion and provides better glycemic control with less hypoglycemia than sliding scale alone, which is reactive and has been associated with worse outcomes in hospitalized patients. Holding all insulin risks ketoacidosis and rebound hyperglycemia, and basal-only regimens leave prandial needs uncovered when the patient eats.
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted to the medical-surgical unit with pneumonia. He is eating about half his meals. Which inpatient insulin strategy is preferred?

options: Place a nasogastric tube and begin gastric lavage with iced saline.
Establish two large-bore IV lines, type and crossmatch blood, keep the patient NPO, and monitor vital signs continuously.
Administer an oral proton pump inhibitor and encourage clear fluids.
Give a Fleet enema to clear blood from the colon before endoscopy.
rationale: Melena with tachycardia, hypotension, and an elevated BUN-to-creatinine ratio indicates a significant upper GI bleed with hemodynamic compromise, so the priority is large-bore IV access, blood availability, NPO status, and continuous monitoring. Iced saline lavage does not improve outcomes and delays resuscitation, oral medications and fluids are unsafe with active bleeding, and enemas are contraindicated and irrelevant to an upper bleed.
stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of NSAID use presents to the ED with black, tarry stools and lightheadedness. Vital signs: blood pressure 94/60 mmHg, heart rate 118 bpm. Labs: hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. What is the priority nursing action?

options: Administer ibuprofen for the abdominal discomfort.
Place the patient in Trendelenburg to improve portal blood flow.
Encourage oral fluids to dilute the blood in the stomach.
Protect the airway, start octreotide infusion as ordered, arrange emergent endoscopy, and avoid NSAIDs.
rationale: Variceal bleeding in cirrhosis is life-threatening with high aspiration risk, so airway protection comes first, followed by octreotide to reduce splanchnic blood flow and urgent endoscopic band ligation. NSAIDs worsen bleeding and are contraindicated in cirrhosis, Trendelenburg does not control variceal hemorrhage, and oral fluids risk aspiration in a vomiting, encephalopathic patient.
